name: Freelance Services Proposal
description: A warm editorial proposal system with conversational typography, terracotta emphasis, clear engagement planning, selected-work proof, and decision-ready pricing.
style_guide:
# Freelance Services Proposal

## Visual concept

This English-language style is designed for independent consultants, designers, strategists, writers, and other specialists presenting a tailored client engagement. It balances the clarity of a commercial scope document with the warmth of a small creative studio: generous paper-toned space, conversational headlines, restrained terracotta emphasis, editorial photography, exact delivery planning, and compact commercial detail. Every page should answer one buying question—what has been heard, what will be done, how the work will run, what evidence supports it, and what decision comes next.

## Canvas, grid, and safe area

- Use a fixed `1280 x 720 px` canvas in a 16:9 ratio.
- Keep `64–76 px` side margins and `46–58 px` top and bottom margins. Preserve more open space than a conventional consulting proposal.
- Use a 12-column grid with `18–22 px` gutters. Typical layouts are 7/5 title-plus-portrait, 4/8 objectives-plus-proof, four equal process phases, and three equal work or pricing cards.
- Reserve a shallow metadata row at the top for the proposal label, section, or page number. Use a fine horizontal rule to anchor it.
- Place the primary headline in the upper quarter of the page and keep `28–42 px` between it and the main exhibit.
- Align card edges, timeline markers, table columns, and footer metadata to shared guides. Keep `20–28 px` between major modules and `12–18 px` inside a component.
- Do not fill every grid cell. The warm negative space is part of the independent-studio character.

## Color system

### Core colors

- Warm paper: `#F3EFE7`. Use as the dominant canvas.
- Clean card: `#FCFBF8`. Use for scope, deliverable, proof, and pricing surfaces.
- Charcoal ink: `#211E1A`. Use for headlines, body text, rules, and the dark proof or recommended panel.
- Terracotta: `#B84F27`. Use for italic phrases, step numbers, timeline bars, markers, links, and the primary call to action.

### Supporting colors

- Muted stone: `#8E877E`. Use for secondary copy, labels, metadata, and inactive schedule states.
- Hairline sand: `#D8D1C5`. Use for dividers, card outlines, table rules, and timeline guides.
- Soft clay: `#E7D2C4`. Use for a quiet category field or selected highlight.
- Reverse paper: `#F7F2E9`. Use for type on Charcoal ink panels.

### Usage rules

- Warm paper, Charcoal ink, and Terracotta define the identity. Keep the deck predominantly light even when one panel is dark.
- Terracotta should normally occupy less than 12 percent of a page. Use it for one principal emphasis: a headline phrase, process state, timeline bar, or recommended option.
- Use dark inversion only for proof, recommendation, quotation, or closing-action panels.
- Never rely on color alone for complete, delayed, recommended, or optional states; add labels, symbols, or line treatment.
- Do not introduce cool corporate blue, neon color, decorative gradients, or a rainbow category system.

## Typography

- Primary font: `Inter`, `Aptos`, or `Helvetica Neue`; fallback: `Arial, system-ui, sans-serif`.
- Use one neutral sans-serif family in upright and italic styles. The italic Terracotta phrase is the typographic signature.
- Cover title: `76–104 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `0.92–1.02`; break it into two or three deliberate lines.
- Content headline: `36–48 px`, weight `400–550`, line-height `1.06–1.16`; highlight no more than one short phrase in Terracotta italic.
- Section eyebrow and proposal metadata: `9–12 px`, weight `600–700`, with `1.6–3 px` tracking.
- Card title: `16–21 px`, weight `600–700`.
- Body copy: `12–16 px`, weight `400–500`, line-height `1.35–1.55`.
- Hero metric or price: `34–48 px`, weight `450–600`; keep currency, unit, and billing period visually attached.
- Use tabular numerals for prices, dates, durations, and performance values. Do not shrink type to fit long scope or legal language.

## Layout and components

- Cards are flat rectangular surfaces with square or nearly square corners, an optional `1 px` Hairline sand border, and no shadow.
- Goal rows pair a two-digit Terracotta index with a short client objective and one compact explanation. Limit the sequence to three or four.
- Proof panels use Charcoal ink with Reverse paper text, two or three large measures, and short definitions. Add an evidence or target label when appropriate.
- Process rails use one thin Terracotta line, small circular phase markers, and evenly spaced columns. Each phase contains a verb, duration, and no more than four activities.
- Working-principle strips use a pale neutral field divided into equal columns for cadence, feedback, revisions, and tools.
- Timeline exhibits use a fixed workstream column and a light weekly grid. Terracotta marks primary work, Charcoal ink marks decisions, and muted warm tones mark review or handoff.
- Selected-work cards combine a consistent image crop, a project context label, one result statement, and verified measures.
- Pricing cards use parallel categories across two or three options. Invert the recommended card to Charcoal ink and attach one small Terracotta recommendation tab.

## Charts and data

- Favor KPI blocks, four-phase rails, simple Gantt schedules, before/after comparisons, and directly labeled bars over dashboards.
- Use Terracotta for the proposed path or primary result, Charcoal ink for baselines or committed work, and Muted stone for context.
- Remove unnecessary axes, legends, and grid lines. Direct-label important values, dates, milestones, and dependencies.
- Every result needs a unit, time period, project context, and status such as observed, estimated, target, or illustrative.
- Timelines must distinguish working time, client review, dependencies, decision gates, and handoff. Mark provisional dates as estimates.
- Pricing comparisons must use identical scope categories and disclose currency, billing basis, included revisions, major exclusions, and validity.
- Do not fabricate proof metrics, testimonials, prices, or certainty. If evidence is missing, omit the field or label it clearly as an assumption, option, estimate, or target.

## Page variations

- Cover: an open Warm paper field for the proposal title, one strong editorial image in a Terracotta side field, and a disciplined footer row for prepared-by, prepared-for, issue date, and validity.
- Client goals and success targets: three numbered objectives in a narrow column beside one dominant dark panel containing two or three measurable targets.
- Engagement process and working rhythm: a four-phase horizontal rail across the body and a low strip for cadence, communication, revision, and tool expectations.
- Deliverables and timeline: one dominant workstream schedule with weekly columns and milestone markers, followed by a concise deliverables row.
- Selected work and client voices: three consistent evidence cards followed by a compact dark quotation or lesson strip. Use only documented and permitted client wording.
- Pricing and next steps: compare options on common criteria, emphasize the recommended path once, and close with payment timing, validity, signature, and the immediate next action.

## Imagery and icons

- Use warm, natural editorial photography of the actual practitioner, team, workspace, craft process, deliverable, or client-relevant environment.
- Favor window light, warm wood or plaster tones, restrained depth of field, and candid but professional expressions.
- Crop images as clean rectangles. A cover portrait or working-context image may occupy roughly one third of the canvas.
- Selected-work imagery should show real outputs or settings, use consistent aspect ratios, and remain subordinate to the proposal argument.
- Icons are optional. When needed, use one simple single-color line or solid family.
- Do not use fake logos, unlicensed portraits, handshake clichés, generic laptop flat-lays, or AI-generated imagery presented as client evidence.

## Avoid

- Do not turn the proposal into a generic blue consulting deck, a glossy agency pitch, or a dark technology presentation.
- Do not use glass effects, heavy shadows, large corner radii, decorative blobs, noisy textures, or gradients.
- Do not highlight several unrelated phrases in Terracotta on one page.
- Do not create crowded scope matrices, miniature legal text, or timelines with unreadable weekly detail.
- Do not use vague headings when a conclusion-led sentence can state what the section achieves.
- Do not present optional work as included, an estimate as a commitment, a target as a result, or a synthesized comment as a testimonial.
